title: Natural Regions of the World
tagline: Location, area, climate, natural vegetation and human adaptation across the major natural regions

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Geography unit 'Natural Regions of the World'. The CISCE unit prescribes the aspects to be covered - location, area, climate, natural vegetation and human adaptation - and this chapter treats every region under those five headings. The CISCE unit itself does not print a numbered list of regions, so the eight regions studied here are the standard set taught for this unit and the chapter does not present them as an official enumeration. No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

learningOutcomes: Define a natural region and state the five aspects of it that the syllabus asks for.
Locate each of the eight natural regions by latitude band and by continent.
State the climate and the natural vegetation of each region.
Describe how people have adapted their farming, herding and living to each region.
Compare the regions with one another and place them on a map from memory.

overview.intro: A natural region is a part of the earth's surface within which the relief, the climate, the soil, the natural vegetation and the human way of life are broadly the same, so that the region has a distinct natural identity of its own. The regions are named after their climate or after the vegetation that grows in them, because climate is the master factor: it decides what can be grown, what the soil is like, and therefore what people do for a living. Moving from the Equator towards the poles the chief belts are the equatorial rainforest, the tropical grasslands, the tropical deserts, the monsoon forests of Asia, the Mediterranean lands, the temperate grasslands, the taiga and the tundra. To the north and south of the tundra lie the polar ice caps, which have no natural vegetation and no permanent settlement. The table below and the sections that follow set out each region under the five aspects the syllabus names, so that the whole unit can be revised as a single grid.

blocks.text: The equatorial region lies in the belt from about 0 to 10 degrees north and south of the Equator, which brings it within the equatorial low pressure belt where the converging trade winds rise and produce heavy convectional rain throughout the year. It is one of the widest of the natural regions and it is the belt of the Amazon basin in South America, the Congo basin in Central Africa, and the islands of South-East Asia, including Indonesia and Malaysia, with an extension into the coastal lowlands of Central America. The temperature stands between 25 and 30 degrees Celsius through the whole year, so that there is no real winter and no hot season either, and the humidity is very high. The natural vegetation is the equatorial rainforest, also called the selvas, in which the trees are broad-leaved and evergreen, so that they shed their leaves and grow new ones one leaf at a time instead of dropping them all together.

items.meaning: The top layer of the rainforest, formed by the crowns of the trees that grow close together; it shuts out the sunlight from the layers below.
The few tallest trees that rise above the canopy and reach the light above it.
The layer of smaller plants below the canopy, which have larger and broader leaves to make the most of the little light that reaches them.
A method of farming in which a patch of forest is cleared, cultivated for a few years and then abandoned, so that the people move on to a new patch.

items: The dark and dense understorey, the creepers and lianas that link the trees together, and the epiphytes that grow on the branches make it difficult to move through the forest.

The heavy rainfall and the constant heat encourage tree ferns, palms, rubber, cocoa and cinchona, and the quinine of the cinchona bark and the rubber of the rubber tree were both once gathered from this region.
Because the soil of the rainforest is thin and is quickly exhausted by the heavy rain, shifting cultivation is common, and the deeper soil is used for plantation crops.
The people adapt by hunting and gathering, by shifting cultivation, by plantation agriculture and by working in the mines, where gold, diamonds, bauxite and iron are found.

blocks.text: The tropical grasslands, or savannas, lie mainly between about 7 and 20 degrees north and south of the Equator, on either side of the equatorial forests, and they cover wide areas of Africa, South America, India and northern Australia. The climate has two clear seasons, a hot wet summer, when the sun is directly overhead and the rain is heavy, and a cooler dry winter, when the sun is lower and the air is dry; the rainfall is moderate and falls almost entirely in the summer. Because there is a long dry season, trees cannot form a closed canopy, and the natural vegetation is tall grass with scattered deciduous trees and low bushes. The trees drop their leaves in the dry season, which reduces the loss of water by transpiration. This region is the home of the great herds of wild animals and is called the natural cattle country, because the tall grass and the bushes feed the cattle of the pastoral peoples who move their herds from one grazing ground to another.

items: The lion, the elephant, the giraffe, the zebra and the deer are characteristic animals of the African savanna, and the tiger and the bison are characteristic of the American savanna.
The grass is tall, about 3 metres in the wetter parts of the region, and it is shorter in the drier parts near the desert.
Human adaptation is cattle ranching and pastoralism, together with plantation agriculture and the cultivation of maize, cotton, sugarcane and coffee.
Fire and the teeth of the grazing animals keep the trees down, so the grassland is a natural region in which people and animals have shaped the vegetation together.

blocks.text: The tropical deserts lie in the belt between about 15 and 30 degrees north and south of the Equator, the belt of the subtropical high pressure, where the descending air is dry and the rainfall is scanty and unreliable. The Sahara of North Africa is the largest of them, and the other great ones are the Arabian desert, the desert of south-west Asia, the Kalahari and the Namib of southern Africa, the desert of western Australia and the Sonoran desert of North America. The days are very hot, because the sun is high, and the nights are cool, because the thin, dry air loses its heat quickly, so the range of temperature between day and night is very large; the Sahara is the region of the greatest daily range on earth. The natural vegetation is sparse, and the plants are xerophytes, adapted to the dryness: they have small leaves or no leaves at all, they have thick bark, and many of them store water in their stems. The date palm and the acacia are typical, and in the deserts of the Americas the cactus and the yucca are typical.

items.meaning: A plant adapted to grow in dry conditions, with small or absent leaves, thick bark, and the ability to store water.
A fertile spot in a desert where water is available, either at a spring or where the groundwater reaches the surface.
The moving of livestock from one grazing ground to another in search of water and pasture, in the manner of the desert peoples.

items: The temperature is often above 40 degrees Celsius in the shade in summer, and the Sahara is the hottest region on earth in summer.
The rainfall is below 25 cm in the year and in the Sahara it is often below 12 cm, and it comes in rare, heavy and short-lived downpours rather than as steady rain.
The Sahara is a region of sand dunes, but not all of it is sand; much of it is bare rock, gravel and salt flats, and so the term desert covers several kinds of surface.

Human adaptation is nomadic herding and hunting in the interior, and settled cultivation in the oases and along the rivers, where the water of the Nile and of the Indus and the Tigris and Euphrates is carried by canals and by long underground channels.
The Aswan Dam in Egypt and the Indira Gandhi Canal in India are examples of the large works built to bring water to the dry land.

blocks.text: The monsoon region covers the southern and south-eastern parts of Asia, including most of India, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Thailand and Vietnam, the southern part of China and the islands of the Philippines, together with the northern part of Australia. Its climate is peculiar because it is ruled by the seasonal reversal of the winds. In summer the land heats faster than the sea, low pressure forms over the land and the moist south-west monsoon is drawn inland from the Indian Ocean and the Pacific, and the rain is heavy and continuous. In winter the land cools faster, high pressure forms over the land and the dry north-east monsoon blows from the continent towards the sea, and the weather is dry and mild. The result is a hot summer and a cool or mild winter with one clearly marked rainy season. In the parts of the region with a heavy rainfall the natural vegetation is the tropical evergreen forest, while in the parts with a lower rainfall it is the tropical deciduous forest, the monsoon forest, in which teak and sal shed their leaves in the dry season to avoid waste of water.

items: The monsoon is not simply a local accident of weather but a great sea-to-land wind system that carries the moisture of the warm oceans onto the land, and its arrival and strength decide the harvest.
The eastern coast of India and the coastal side of the Western Ghats receive the heaviest rain, while the interior of the peninsula lies in the rain shadow of the same hills and is much drier.
The natural vegetation of the higher parts of the region is the montane forest, which gives way to alpine meadow and then to snow on the highest ranges of the Himalaya.
Human adaptation is intensive agriculture, rice cultivation, terrace farming on the hills, and the plantation of tea, coffee, jute and sugarcane.

blocks.text: The Mediterranean region lies between about 30 and 45 degrees north and south of the Equator, but only on the western margins of the continents, where the seas and the westerly winds of the middle latitudes meet: the Mediterranean coast of southern Europe, the coast of California, central Chile, the Cape region of South Africa, and the south-west and south of Australia. Its climate is the Mediterranean climate, with warm, dry summers and mild, wet winters, and it is the only region of the world with this rhythm. The cause is the seasonal movement of the pressure belts. In summer the subtropical high pressure belt moves over the region, so the air descends, the weather is hot, dry and clear, and the land is baked hard. In winter the belt moves away, the westerlies bring moist air from the Atlantic, and rain falls on the land. The natural vegetation is made of evergreen shrubs and trees with some deciduous trees: the olive is the commonest tree, and the cork oak, the laurel, the oleander, the pine and the citrus are characteristic, together with wild grasses and scrub.

items: The narrow coastal strip and the islands of the Mediterranean, together with the narrow strips of the other west-coast regions, make this the smallest of the eight regions by area.
The dry summer means that the ground is baked and hard and that fires are a danger, which is why the vegetation is scrubby and fires are a feature of the summer landscape.

Human adaptation is orchard farming on the irrigated, well-drained slopes, with grapes, olives and citrus fruits, together with horticulture, and in the Mediterranean lands tourism has become an important occupation.
The winter rain suits the growth of winter crops such as wheat and barley, which are sown after the harvest and ripen before the dry summer begins.

blocks.text: The temperate grasslands form broad belts in the interior of the continents between about 40 and 55 degrees north and south of the Equator, away from the wetter coasts and from the dry interiors of the continents. They are called the Prairies in North America, the Pampas in South America, the Downs in Australia, the Veld in South Africa and the Steppes in Eurasia, and they are among the most fertile lands in the world, which is why they have been called the granaries of the world. The climate is continental, with moderate rainfall, hot summers and cold winters, and it becomes drier towards the interior. The natural vegetation is tall grass in the wetter parts and short grass in the drier parts. The soil is deep and fertile; in the Prairies and the Steppes it is the black chernozem soil, rich in humus, which was formed under the natural grass cover.

items: The grasslands are the region of the great wheat and maize belts, and they also carry vast herds of cattle and sheep.
The farming is extensive rather than intensive, and it is carried on large holdings with machinery, so the population is thin and scattered.
In the wetter east of the Prairies the tall grass used to grow so high that a rider on horseback could not be seen, which is why they were called the tall-grass country.

Human adaptation is extensive wheat cultivation, the rearing of cattle and sheep, and the mining of coal and the oil of the mid-continent, and in the Pampas the wheat and beef of Argentina and Uruguay.

learn.title: The Taiga Region and the Tundra Region

blocks.text: The taiga, the coniferous or boreal forest, forms a broad belt between about 55 and 70 degrees north of the Equator across Canada, Alaska, Scandinavia and Russia, and it is also known as the cool temperate continental or Siberian type of climate. The winters are long and severe and the summers are short, cool and comparatively dry. The natural vegetation is evergreen coniferous forest of spruce, pine and fir, with birch and aspen in the clearer parts, and larch which sheds its needles in the winter. The tundra lies beyond it, mainly north of the Arctic Circle in northern Canada, Alaska, Greenland, northern Scandinavia and northern Russia, and it also occurs on the coast of Antarctica. Its climate is the polar type: the winters are long and severe and the summers are short and cool, the temperature in the warmest month seldom rises above 10 degrees Celsius, and in mid-winter it may fall to minus 37 degrees Celsius. No tree can grow here, and the natural vegetation is only mosses, lichens, and dwarf willows and birches that creep along the ground.

blocks.caption: Table: the taiga and the tundra compared
rows: About 55 to 70 degrees north, in Canada, Alaska, Scandinavia and Russia
North of the Arctic Circle, in northern Canada, Alaska, Greenland, Scandinavia and Russia
Long severe winters, short cool summers, moderate rainfall
Polar climate, long severe winters, cool brief summers, down to about -37 degrees Celsius
Evergreen coniferous forest of spruce, pine and fir, with birch, aspen and larch
Mosses, lichens and dwarf willows and birches; no trees
Sparsely populated; forestry, mining, and crops such as barley, oats, rye, potatoes and beetroot
Very sparsely populated; reindeer herding, hunting, fishing, and mining with pipelines and roads

items: North of the tundra lie the polar ice caps of Greenland and Antarctica, which have no vegetation at all and no permanent settlement.
The permafrost, the permanently frozen subsoil of the tundra, cannot be built on and cannot be ploughed, and it keeps the soil waterlogged in summer.
The coniferous forests of the taiga give the world its softwood, timber, pulp and paper, and the fur-bearing animals of the cold north have always supported hunting peoples.
The peoples of the far north live in tents or in small permanent settlements and move with the reindeer, and the sled with its dogs is still the usual means of travel.

keyPoints: A natural region is a part of the earth's surface with a uniform relief, climate, soil, vegetation and way of life.
The syllabus asks for each region under five headings: location, area, climate, natural vegetation and human adaptation.
Climate is the master factor, because it decides the soil, the vegetation and the human occupation.
The Equatorial region lies within about 10 degrees of the Equator, with a temperature of 25 to 30 degrees Celsius and rain throughout the year.
The equatorial rainforest is the selvas, with a canopy, an emergent layer and an understorey.
The Tropical Grasslands, or savannas, have a hot wet summer and a cool dry winter, and are the natural cattle country.
The Tropical Deserts lie in the subtropical high pressure belt, have a very large daily range of temperature and carry xerophytes.
The Tropical Monsoon region of southern and south-eastern Asia has one clearly marked rainy season and a tropical deciduous forest.
The Mediterranean region has warm dry summers and mild wet winters, and its commonest tree is the olive.
The Temperate Grasslands, or Prairies, Pampas, Downs, Veld and Steppes, are the granaries of the world.
The Taiga is the coniferous forest belt between 55 and 70 degrees north, and the Tundra lies beyond it with only mosses and lichens.
Human adaptation is the clearest link between the climate of a region and the way its people live.
examFocus: A question on any region usually asks for its location, climate, vegetation and human adaptation, so learn the four together for each one.
Questions ask for the names of the natural regions, so keep the eight names and their latitudes ready, and remember that the grassland regions have different names in different continents.
Comparisons between the equatorial region and the tropical grasslands, or between the taiga and the tundra, are common, and in each the difference is usually the rainfall and the vegetation.
For a question on human adaptation, name the occupation and say what makes it possible, for example shifting cultivation in the equatorial region because the soil is exhausted quickly.
A location question wants the latitude band and the continent, and the answer is improved by naming one region on another continent.

vocabulary.meaning: A part of the earth's surface with a broadly uniform relief, climate, soil, vegetation and human life.
The equatorial rainforest of the Amazon and Congo basins.
The tropical grassland of the regions between the equatorial forest and the desert.
A plant adapted to dry conditions.
A fertile spot in a desert where water is available.
The deep, fertile black soil of the temperate grasslands.
The coniferous forest belt of the cool temperate continental or Siberian type of climate.
The polar region north of the Arctic Circle, with mosses, lichens and dwarf bushes.
The permanently frozen subsoil of the tundra.

questions.prompt: The natural region lying within about 10 degrees of the Equator is the:
questions.explanation: The equatorial region lies in the belt from about 0 to 10 degrees north and south of the Equator, within the equatorial low pressure belt, and is the belt of the selvas.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the tropical grassland, which lies beyond it, from about 7 to 20 degrees from the Equator.

questions.prompt: The temperate grasslands of Australia are called the:
questions.explanation: The same natural region is called the Prairies in North America, the Pampas in South America, the Veld in South Africa and the Steppes in Eurasia, and the Downs in Australia.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the Veld, which is the name of the same region in South Africa.

questions.prompt: Plants that are adapted to grow in arid conditions are called:
questions.explanation: Xerophytes have small or absent leaves, thick bark and the ability to store water, so that they can live in the dry conditions of the desert.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing epiphytes, which are plants that grow upon other plants for support in the damp equatorial forest.

questions.prompt: The climate with warm dry summers and mild wet winters is the:
questions.explanation: The Mediterranean climate is the only one with this rhythm, and it is caused by the seasonal movement of the subtropical high pressure belt over the region in summer and away from it in winter, when the westerlies bring the rain.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the tropical monsoon climate, which has one rainy season and a long dry season instead of a mild rainy winter.

questions.prompt: The region known as the natural cattle country of the world is the:
questions.explanation: The savanna is the natural cattle country, because its tall grass and bushes feed the large herds of the pastoral peoples who move their cattle between grazing grounds.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the taiga, which is forested and is the region of the fur-bearing animals.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the commonest tree of the Mediterranean region is the ______.
questions.explanation: The olive is the commonest tree of the Mediterranean region, and it is grown in the orchards along with the grape vine and the citrus trees. Cork oak, laurel and pine are the other characteristic trees.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 'cork oak', which is characteristic of the region but is not the commonest tree.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the coniferous forest belt of the cool temperate continental or Siberian type of climate is called the ______.
questions.explanation: The taiga is the coniferous forest belt between about 55 and 70 degrees north, and it is also known as the Siberian type of climate region.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 'tundra', which lies beyond the taiga and has no trees at all.

questions.prompt: State the location, climate, natural vegetation and human adaptation of the Equatorial region.
questions.answer: Location: it lies in the belt from about 0 to 10 degrees north and south of the Equator, covering the Amazon basin of South America, the Congo basin of Central Africa, the islands of South-East Asia and the coastal lowlands of Central America. Climate: the temperature is between 25 and 30 degrees Celsius throughout the year, with no real winter, the humidity is very high, and the rainfall is heavy and convectional in every month because the region lies in the equatorial low pressure belt. Natural vegetation: the equatorial rainforest, or selvas, of broad-leaved evergreen trees, arranged in an emergent layer above a closed canopy, with a dense understorey of ferns and creepers and lianas linking the trees together. Human adaptation: hunting and gathering, shifting cultivation in which a patch of forest is cleared and cultivated for a few years and then abandoned, plantation agriculture, and mining.
questions.explanation: The four headings of the syllabus are used and each is answered with the facts that belong to the equatorial region.
questions.commonMistake: Describing the climate of the equatorial region with a rainy season and a dry season, which belongs to the monsoon and the savanna regions.

questions.prompt: Explain why the Tropical Deserts have a very large difference in temperature between day and night, and describe how the people of the Sahara have adapted to the desert.
questions.answer: The days are hot because the sun is high above the horizon and the air is clear and cloudless, so the ground receives the full strength of the sunlight. The nights are cool because the desert air is very dry and thin, and dry air and a cloudless sky lose their heat quickly once the sun has set, so the ground cools rapidly. The result is a very large daily range of temperature, and the Sahara is the region of the greatest range on earth. The people have adapted in several ways. In the interior, where there is no water, they follow the herds of goats, sheep and camels from one grazing ground to another in nomadic herding, and they hunt and gather the fruit of the desert plants. Where water is available, in the oases and along the Nile and the other rivers of the region, they have settled and cultivated the land, growing barley, wheat, cotton, sugarcane, dates and vegetables. To bring water to the dry land they have built works of great size, such as the Aswan Dam on the Nile and the Indira Gandhi Canal in India, and in the older settlements they use underground channels that carry the water from the mountains to the fields. So the adaptation is of two kinds, moving with the herds where there is no water, and settling and irrigating where there is.
questions.explanation: The cause of the temperature range and the two forms of human adaptation both have to be made explicit.
questions.commonMistake: Giving only the oasis cultivation and leaving out the nomadic herding of the interior, which is the more characteristic adaptation of the Sahara.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between the taiga and the tundra in their location, vegetation and human activities.
questions.answer: Location: the taiga lies between about 55 and 70 degrees north, across Canada, Alaska, Scandinavia and Russia, while the tundra lies north of the Arctic Circle in northern Canada, Alaska, Greenland, northern Scandinavia and northern Russia, and also on the coast of Antarctica. Vegetation: the taiga is the coniferous forest of spruce, pine and fir, with birch, aspen and larch in the clearer parts, while the tundra has no trees at all and carries only mosses, lichens and dwarf willows and birches that creep along the ground, because the subsoil is permanently frozen and the summer is too short and too cool for a tree to grow. Human activities: the taiga is thinly peopled, and the people work in forestry, in mining and in small-scale farming of barley, oats, rye, potatoes and beetroot, and the softwood of the forests supplies the world with timber, pulp and paper. The tundra is very thinly peopled, and the people keep reindeer, hunt and fish, and the modern settlements serve the mines of oil, gas and minerals, which are joined to the coast by roads and pipelines. In both regions the settlements are few and scattered, and the occupations depend on the cold and on the thin soil, but the taiga has a forest to work in and the tundra has only the tundra itself.
questions.explanation: The comparison needs a point under each of the three headings and the same order for both regions.
questions.commonMistake: Saying that the tundra has coniferous forests, which places the taiga in the wrong region.

questions.prompt: Compare the Tropical Grasslands and the Temperate Grasslands in their location, climate, vegetation, soil and human adaptation.
questions.answer: Location: the tropical grasslands, or savannas, lie mainly between about 7 and 20 degrees north and south of the Equator, on either side of the equatorial forests, and cover wide parts of Africa, South America, India and northern Australia. The temperate grasslands form broad belts in the interior of the continents between about 40 and 55 degrees north and south, and are called the Prairies in North America, the Pampas in South America, the Downs in Australia, the Veld in South Africa and the Steppes in Eurasia. Climate: the tropical grasslands have two sharply marked seasons, a hot wet summer and a cooler dry winter, with the rain falling almost entirely in the summer. The temperate grasslands have a continental climate of moderate rainfall with hot summers and cold winters, and the rainfall decreases towards the dry interior of the continent. Vegetation: in the tropical grasslands the tall grass grows with scattered deciduous trees and low bushes, and the trees shed their leaves in the dry season, and in the wetter parts the grass is about 3 metres high. In the temperate grasslands the grass is tall in the wetter parts and short in the drier parts, and there are hardly any trees, except where the rainfall is higher. Soil: the tropical grassland soil is less fertile, because the heavy rain washes out the nutrients and the soil is often red, while the temperate grassland soil is deep and very fertile, the black chernozem of the Prairies and the Steppes, rich in humus formed under the natural grass cover, which is why these are among the most fertile lands in the world. Human adaptation: in the tropical grasslands the occupation is cattle ranching and pastoralism, with the herds moved between grazing grounds, together with plantation agriculture and the growing of maize, cotton, sugarcane and coffee. In the temperate grasslands it is extensive wheat cultivation over large holdings worked by machinery, the rearing of cattle and sheep, and the mining of coal and oil, and the region is the granary of the world because of the fertility of its soil. The essential difference is that the tropical grassland is a region of the same grass but of a poorer soil and a wetter summer, whereas the temperate grassland has the better soil and the colder winter.
questions.explanation: A comparison of five headings is expected, and the closing sentence should name what actually distinguishes the two.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing the two grasslands by giving the summer rain of the savanna and the fertile black soil of the temperate grassland to the same region.

questions.prompt: Explain what a natural region is, why the natural regions of the world are named after climate or vegetation, and describe the human adaptation of the Mediterranean region.
questions.answer: A natural region is a part of the earth's surface within which the relief, the climate, the soil, the natural vegetation and the human way of life are broadly uniform, so that the region has a distinct natural identity. The natural regions are named after their climate or after the vegetation that grows in them, for example the equatorial rainforest, the savanna and the taiga, because climate is the master factor. Climate decides the amount of heat and the supply of water, and through them it decides the kind of soil that forms, the vegetation that can grow, and the crops and the animals that people can keep, so that a region with a similar climate has a similar natural cover and a similar human occupation. The Mediterranean region lies between about 30 and 45 degrees north and south of the Equator, but only on the western margins of the continents, in southern Europe, California, central Chile, the Cape of South Africa and the south-west and south of Australia. Its climate has warm dry summers and mild wet winters, and the vegetation is of evergreen shrubs and trees with some deciduous trees, the olive, the cork oak, the laurel, the pine and the citrus, together with wild grasses and scrub. The people have adapted to the dry summer and the mild wet winter in several ways. The chief occupation is orchard farming on the slopes, with grapes for wine and dried fruit, olives for oil, and the citrus fruits of oranges and lemons, and the mild winter suits horticulture and the growing of vegetables and flowers. Winter wheat and barley are sown after the autumn harvest and ripen before the dry summer begins. Because the summer ground is baked hard, the farming is carried out on the better-drained and irrigated slopes rather than in the lowlands, and the narrow coastal strip is also the region that attracts the greatest number of tourists, so that tourism has become an important source of income. The thin soils and the dry summers also explain the scrubby vegetation, and fires are a feature of the summer landscape.
questions.explanation: The definition, the reason for the naming and the four-part account of the Mediterranean region all have to be present.
questions.commonMistake: Describing the Mediterranean climate with a wet summer and a dry winter, which is the climate of the monsoon region.

questions.prompt: Two students claim that 'a natural region is simply a part of the world that has a name'. Examine this claim and show, with examples from the natural regions, what the idea of a natural region actually means.
questions.answer: The claim confuses a name with a definition. A region is not a region because it has a name, and the name is only a label for a set of physical features that are alike. A natural region is a part of the earth's surface within which the relief, the climate, the soil, the natural vegetation and the human way of life are broadly the same, so that the whole area has a distinct natural identity of its own. The test of a natural region is therefore that its parts resemble one another and differ from those of its neighbours, and the name is simply the label that the geographer gives to that combination. Three examples show how the definition works. The Equatorial region is named for its climate, because the temperature of 25 to 30 degrees Celsius and the heavy convectional rain of every month produce the selvas of the Amazon and Congo basins, and the same combination of heat and rain produces the same human adaptation of shifting cultivation and plantation agriculture in Africa, in South America and in South-East Asia. The Mediterranean region is named for its position, and it exists only on the western margins of the continents because only there do the subtropical high pressure belt of summer and the westerlies of winter meet, which gives the warm dry summer and mild wet winter and with it the evergreen scrub, the olive and the orchard farming of southern Europe, of California and of central Chile. The taiga is named for its vegetation, the evergreen coniferous forest, and the cool temperate continental climate between 55 and 70 degrees north gives that forest and the forestry and mining that go with it, whether it is in Canada, in Scandinavia or in Siberia. The definition also has a practical value, which is that once the region is understood, the human activity of the region can be predicted from the climate. That is why the syllabus asks for the location, area, climate, natural vegetation and human adaptation of each region in that order: the chain runs from the climate to the vegetation and the soil, and from those to the way people live. So the student is right that the regions have names, but the names are the conclusion of the reasoning and not the reasoning itself.
questions.explanation: The answer has to give a working definition, test it against three named regions and show that the names follow from the physical facts.
questions.commonMistake: Answering with a list of the eight regions only, without showing that the definition of a natural region is what makes them regions.
